title: The Montreal ozone treaty was the first in UN history to be ratified by every country
body: Ozone high in the atmosphere is Earth's natural sunscreen, shielding life from the Sun's ultraviolet light. In the early 1970s [scientists recognised](https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/31392/) that CFCs, chemicals then used as refrigerants and in spray cans, could destroy it, and by the 1980s a hole was opening over Antarctica every southern spring. In 1987 governments agreed the **Montreal Protocol** to phase out CFCs and similar chemicals; it now has 198 parties, every UN member and a few more, the first universally ratified treaty in UN history. Ozone levels have been fairly stable since the mid-1990s, and a 2022 assessment projects that ozone over Antarctica will be back to 1980 levels by about 2066.

slides.alt: Antarctica seen from above, one frame per year from 1979 to 2025. A deep blue and purple hole of low ozone grows over the continent through the 1980s and stays large, while a graph beside it climbs from near zero and then levels off with ups and downs.
slides.caption: The ozone hole on its biggest day of each year, 1979 to 2025, sped up 1.5×. Blue and purple mark the least ozone. The graph's peak areas run from 1.1 to 29.9 million km².

slides.heading: The ozone hole on its biggest day of the year
slides.note: From NASA's satellite record; 2025 peaked on 9 September

slides.text: Perhaps the single most successful international agreement to date has been the Montreal Protocol.

slides.note: Projections from the 2022 scientific assessment of ozone depletion

slides.question: Look at the dates in the clip. When does the ozone hole reach its biggest each year?
slides.explanation: It peaks in the southern spring, in September or early October. In 2025 the hole was biggest on 9 September, at 22.86 million km².
